terms.definition: A cloud execution model where the provider manages server infrastructure entirely. You provide code and a trigger; AWS handles provisioning, scaling, patching, and availability.
terms.example: Lambda, DynamoDB, and S3 are all serverless — you never configure or maintain the underlying servers.

terms.definition: AWS's serverless compute service. You upload code (called a function), define a trigger, and Lambda executes the code on demand in an ephemeral container — billing you per millisecond of execution.
terms.example: The Load-Inventory function runs only when a CSV file is uploaded to S3, then stops. No server runs between uploads.

terms.definition: The initialization delay that occurs when Lambda must create and configure a new execution container for a function that has no warm container available. Adds milliseconds to seconds of latency.
terms.example: Todd's bot failed because the cold start plus model processing pushed the response past API Gateway's 29-second timeout.

terms.definition: An IAM role attached to a Lambda function that grants it permissions to call other AWS services on your behalf during execution. Required for every Lambda function.
terms.example: Lambda-Load-Inventory-Role grants the Load-Inventory function permission to read from S3 and write to DynamoDB.

terms.definition: A configuration that connects an AWS event source (like DynamoDB Streams, SQS, or Kinesis) to a Lambda function, causing Lambda to be invoked when new records arrive.
terms.example: The DynamoDB Streams event source mapping triggers Check-Stock whenever items are written to the Inventory table.

terms.definition: A time-ordered log of item-level changes in a DynamoDB table. Each change (insert, update, delete) is captured and made available for up to 24 hours. Can trigger Lambda functions.
terms.example: When Load-Inventory writes a new inventory row, DynamoDB Streams captures it and immediately triggers Check-Stock.

terms.definition: A configuration on an S3 bucket that fires a notification (to Lambda, SNS, or SQS) when specific events occur — such as object creation (upload), deletion, or restoration.
terms.example: The inventory bucket is configured to invoke Load-Inventory Lambda whenever any file is uploaded (s3:ObjectCreated:*).

terms.definition: A named communication channel in Amazon SNS. Publishers send messages to a topic; SNS distributes the message to all subscribers simultaneously.
terms.example: The 'NoStock' topic receives out-of-stock alerts from Check-Stock Lambda and fans them out to all subscribers (email, SMS, etc.).

terms.definition: Publish/Subscribe — a messaging pattern where publishers send messages to a topic without knowing who receives them, and subscribers receive all messages published to topics they've subscribed to.
terms.example: Check-Stock publishes to the NoStock topic; your email address is a subscriber. Add 10 more email subscribers — all receive the same alert without changing any code.

terms.definition: The primary attribute in a DynamoDB table, used to distribute data across partitions. Every item must have a partition key value. Together with a sort key (if defined), it forms the composite primary key.
terms.example: In the Inventory table, Store is the partition key — all items for Berlin go to the same partition.

terms.definition: An optional secondary attribute in DynamoDB's primary key. When combined with a partition key, each item's combination of both values must be unique. Enables range queries within a partition.
terms.example: In the Inventory table, Item is the sort key — Berlin/Echo Dot and Berlin/Echo Show are two different items in the same partition.

terms.definition: Identical to Execution Role — the IAM role a Lambda function assumes during invocation to gain temporary credentials for accessing other AWS resources.
terms.example: Without an execution role with DynamoDB write permissions, the Load-Inventory Lambda would receive an AccessDeniedException when trying to call put_item.

terms.definition: A Lambda feature that keeps a specified number of execution environments initialized and ready to respond instantly, eliminating cold start latency for latency-sensitive applications.
terms.example: A checkout API that must respond within 100ms would use Provisioned Concurrency to ensure no cold start delay during peak shopping hours.

terms.definition: The maximum amount of time a Lambda function is allowed to run before AWS forcibly terminates it. Configurable from 1 second to 15 minutes. Defaults to 3 seconds.
terms.example: If Load-Inventory takes 25 seconds to process a huge CSV file but timeout is set to 10 seconds, the function will be killed mid-execution.

terms.definition: The official AWS SDK for Python. Used in Lambda functions to interact with AWS services programmatically — creating DynamoDB connections, reading S3 objects, publishing SNS messages.
terms.example: In Load-Inventory: boto3.resource('dynamodb') creates a DynamoDB connection; in Check-Stock: boto3.client('sns') creates an SNS client.

terms.definition: A DynamoDB billing mode (PAY_PER_REQUEST) where you pay per read/write request with no capacity planning required. Scales automatically. Best for unpredictable workloads.
terms.example: Perfect for this lab's inventory system — only charges when files are actually uploaded and data is read, not for idle time.

terms.definition: The security principle of granting only the minimum permissions necessary for a task — nothing more. Critical for Lambda execution roles in production.
terms.example: Instead of AmazonDynamoDBFullAccess, production Load-Inventory should have a custom policy allowing only dynamodb:PutItem on the specific Inventory table ARN.

terms.definition: API Gateway enforces a hard maximum response timeout of 29 seconds that cannot be increased. Any Lambda function invoked through API Gateway that doesn't respond within 29 seconds will receive a 504 Gateway Timeout error on the client side.
terms.example: Todd's AI bot Lambda ran for 31 seconds successfully, but API Gateway already returned an error to the user at second 29.

terms.definition: A collection of AWS resources defined in a CloudFormation template and managed as a single unit. Create, update, and delete all resources together with a single operation.
terms.example: The personal account CloudFormation template in this lab creates the DynamoDB table, S3 bucket, and both IAM roles as a single stack — deployable and teardown-able in one command.

terms.definition: AWS's identity service for application end-users. Provides user pools (authentication) and identity pools (authorization/temporary AWS credentials) for apps — without creating IAM users.
terms.example: The Inventory Dashboard uses a Cognito identity pool to get temporary read-only DynamoDB credentials for the browser — no IAM user or login required.

terms.definition: A DynamoDB API operation that creates a new item or completely replaces an existing item with the same primary key. Used in the Load-Inventory Lambda to write each CSV row.
terms.example: inventoryTable.put_item(Item={'Store': 'Berlin', 'Item': 'Echo Dot', 'Count': 12}) writes one row to the Inventory table.

terms.definition: The unique Amazon Resource Name (ARN) identifying a DynamoDB Stream. Required when creating a Lambda event source mapping to connect the stream to a Lambda function.
terms.example: When creating the DynamoDB Streams trigger for Check-Stock via CLI, you must provide the Stream ARN (not the table ARN).

terms.definition: In a Lambda DynamoDB Streams event source mapping, the maximum number of stream records sent to Lambda in a single invocation. Default is 100; max is 10,000.
terms.example: If 500 records change in DynamoDB and batch size is 100, Lambda will be invoked 5 times, each receiving 100 records.
